proposals.hypothesis: Question: which representation choices of the hourly rental signal actually transfer forward, rather than merely interpolating inside the training period? The measured development leader (action d81da712963c24b0e0581c92881e88ef6155ce721f33df1a06d438b0f13e3d90, task idea-baseline-2, dev RMSE 59.993, equal-date MAE 40.955) is a raw-feature HistGradientBoosting on counts with elapsed_day included; the linear reference (idea-baseline-1, 182.95) and median reference (idea-baseline-0, 268.48) show that most of the signal is nonlinear hour/weather structure, which changed my prior view that a linear trend term would carry much weight. Two competing expectations are tested here and stated before execution: (a) log1p target modelling helps, because hourly counts are heteroscedastic and multiplicative in hour-of-day, so relative-error fitting should generalise into a later, higher-volume period; (b) log1p target hurts row RMSE, because RMSE is dominated by the high-count commute peaks that a log fit systematically under-weights, and because expm1 back-transform is biased low. Similarly, (c) elapsed_day is useful calendar information, versus (d) elapsed_day is harmful for forward transfer because a tree cannot extrapolate beyond the train maximum and will flatten the 2012 growth into a constant last-bin offset, so dropping it and relying on yr/mnth/season may transfer better. Rather than assert either side, the program measures all eight combinations (elapsed on/off x raw/log target x reference-capacity/deeper-slower HGB) on two strictly chronological 61-day internal holdouts carved from train only (approximating the 61-day development window), selects the lowest mean RMSE branch, refits on all supplied training rows and reports the actually selected branch, fold RMSEs and any fallback in findings. Expected informative outcomes: if the selected branch is 'elapsed|raw|ref' and dev RMSE is not better than 59.993, that is a negative result showing the added cyclical/interaction features and capacity change do not transfer; if a no-elapsed or log branch wins internally but loses on development, that is direct evidence that an internal chronological holdout in March-April does not proxy May-June transfer, which matters for the later confirmation split. Program-authored findings can still be wrong; only the independent development score is a measurement.

proposals.hypothesis: Question: does an explicit daily-level growth component (estimated in log space on daily mean counts, with annual harmonics to separate trend from seasonality) transfer better into a later period than the implicit, non-extrapolating level encoding a tree learns from elapsed_day/yr? Prior evidence changed my view twice. (1) idea-baseline-2 (plain HGB on all raw columns, dev RMSE 59.99) beat idea-4ed689 (dev RMSE 62.03), whose internal 2-fold chronological selection chose 'noelapsed|raw|ref' although its own folds disagreed sharply (89.5 vs 101.3 for the chosen branch, 115.1 vs 80.1 for the elapsed branch). So 2-fold selection was too noisy to rank transfer, and dropping elapsed_day was actually harmful on the real May-June 2012 period even though 100% of evaluation rows lie beyond the training elapsed_day range. (2) All log-target branches in idea-4ed689 were clearly worse under row RMSE (111.9/107.2 vs 97.6/98.3), so I avoid fitting in log space and instead fit a ratio target y/g(d) with sample weights g(d)^2, which keeps the raw-scale squared-error weighting while removing the level. Contrasting expected outcomes: (a) if the 2011->2012 growth is a smooth level trend that continues past 2012-04-30, the 'trend_full' branch (linear log-trend extrapolated) should beat the fixed baseline on all four 40-date chronological holdouts and give dev RMSE clearly below 59.99; (b) if the trees' implicit last-level plateau is already adequate (or growth saturates), 'trend_frozen' (level clamped at the last training day) should win and behave near baseline; (c) if neither passes the guard (mean RMSE below baseline AND wins in >=3 of 4 folds) the program keeps the exact baseline-2 configuration and should reproduce ~60 dev RMSE, which would be an informative negative result showing the growth relationship is already captured by elapsed_day splits and needs no explicit extrapolation. The guard directly encodes the lesson that a noisy internal ranking can flip to a worse model. Unverified: the harmonic-plus-linear trend fit on only ~16 months may confound trend with annual seasonality; the reported slope and fold table are the diagnostics that would decide this.

scientific_limits: Weighted ratio loss corresponds to raw squared residuals for fixed g, but regularization and early stopping mean it is not equivalent to ordinary raw HGB.

proposals.hypothesis: Question: does the parent's explicit multiplicative level representation (daily log-linear + annual/semiannual harmonic trend, ratio target y/g with weights g^2, elapsed_day dropped, level frozen at the last training day for out-of-range days) actually transfer to the later period, or was its apparent advantage an artifact of a few internal fold blocks? Prior evidence changed my view about what has been measured: in idea-7637c7 the trend_frozen challenger had a clearly lower mean internal fold RMSE (56.735 vs baseline 65.254) but won only 2 of 4 chronological folds (fold RMSE baseline [56.555, 81.425, 63.177, 59.857] vs trend_frozen [57.765, 57.564, 40.626, 70.985]), so the >=3-win gate selected the fixed baseline; consequently the measured development loss 59.976 is essentially the reference HistGradientBoosting number (59.993 for idea-baseline-2), and the trend representation itself has never been scored on development. Contrasting expected outcomes stated before execution: (A) if end-of-train level freezing genuinely fixes the level dilution that raw-elapsed_day trees suffer, development row RMSE should land near or below ~57 with equal-date MAE not worse than ~41, and the representation becomes the base for further work (e.g. Poisson/log-count loss, hour x workingday profile terms); (B) if the fold gains were block-specific (folds 2-3 only), development RMSE should come out at or above ~61-62 with a higher prediction mean bias, which would be an informative negative result showing the raw-feature HGB already encodes the 2012 level adequately via the yr and binned elapsed_day splits, and the remaining rounds should instead target loss/target transformation or hour-profile structure rather than global level modelling. Diagnostics added this round (reference baseline prediction mean, mean absolute prediction difference, and what the old win-count rule would have chosen) are computed but do not influence the returned vector, so the score is attributable to the unconditional trend_frozen branch. Unverified expectation: the frozen level factor is a single constant multiplier for all development rows (kappa=0 with all inputs beyond train elapsed max), so any systematic level error should show up as a near-uniform scale bias rather than shape error.

proposals.hypothesis: Question: why did the frozen-trend ratio representation (idea-e79ce2, action e58e...? no — action 042b6227..., dev RMSE 85.34, pred_mean 324.2 vs 271.6 for the raw HGB) lose badly on May–June 2012 development even though its own four chronological 40-date training folds preferred it (mean 56.7 vs baseline 65.3), and is the currently leading program (idea-7637c7, dev RMSE 59.976) merely the raw reference HGB branch that its own selection rule kept? Only an analyze action can see development labels, so this round measures directly what methods cannot. Contrasting expected outcomes stated before execution: (A) LEVEL-ERROR explanation — the multiplicative level frozen at the last training day overshoots the actual May–June level, so trend_k0 will show opt_scale clearly below 1 (roughly 0.82-0.90) and rmse_opt_scale falling back near ~60, meaning the hour/weather shape learned on the ratio target is fine and only the extrapolated level factor is wrong; (B) SHAPE-DISTORTION explanation — the g^2 sample weights concentrate the fit on late, high-volume dates and distort the diurnal profile, so rescaling recovers little (rmse_opt_scale still >70) and hourly residuals of the ratio model differ structurally from the raw baseline; (C) both partly true. Second question: does any alternative target representation transfer better than the raw-target reference HGB — log1p target, Poisson loss, elapsed_day removed, and simple 50/50 blends — measured under two protocols (train->development future transfer, and a held-out last-61-training-day internal block). Contrasting expectation: if internal chronological holdout ranking reproduces the development ranking, internal validation is a usable selection proxy; if the rankings disagree at the top (as the e79ce2 contradiction suggests), any future-period selection rule built only from training-internal folds is unreliable and later rounds must prefer conservative representations. How prior evidence changed my view: before e79ce2 I expected a fitted growth trend to help because 2011->2012 growth is large; the measured 85.34 (42% worse than baseline) contradicted that, so I no longer trust the internal-fold preference and want the level/shape split quantified before spending the remaining method rounds. This action returns findings only (prediction is null), so it does not affect the leaderboard; the fallback default selection remains the measured 59.976 leader.

proposals.hypothesis: Question: does modelling hourly counts multiplicatively (log1p target) transfer better into a later period than the raw-target reference, and is a retransformation (Jensen) bias correction estimated on interpolation folds safe to apply? Prior evidence changed my view twice. (1) The measured leader idea-7637c7 (raw-target reference HGB, dev RMSE 59.976) selects its baseline branch through strictly chronological 40-date training blocks; the diagnostic run idea-845571 reports that this internal design ranks candidates almost inversely to actual train->development transfer (rank_internal top trend_k0, hgb_log last; rank_dev top hgb_log 52.712 / date_mae 35.253 vs hgb_raw 59.976 / 40.878; internal_top_is_dev_top false). The internal last-61-day block sits in the rising spring season, so every no-elapsed/shrinking model is punished by level bias (opt_scale 1.5-1.8) rather than by shape error — that is a seasonal confound, not a transfer measurement. I therefore expect an internal-holdout selector to be a poor selector here and fix the branch a priori instead. (2) hgb_log under-predicted the development level slightly (pred_mean 265.33 vs dev mean 272.33, opt_scale 1.0279, rmse_opt_scale 51.874), which is the signature of expm1 retransformation bias, a within-distribution estimation issue rather than a future-period question; so I estimate it with random-date (interpolation) folds and clip it to [1.00,1.10] to prevent the trend-confounded 1.5-1.8 ratios from leaking in. Contrasting expected outcomes: (a) log-target transfers better and dev RMSE lands near 52-55, clearly beating 59.976, with the bias factor small (<1.05) and slightly helpful; (b) my reimplementation differs from the diagnostic's hgb_log and lands at/above 60, meaning the reported dev advantage was implementation-specific and multiplicative structure does not by itself transfer; (c) the interpolation-estimated factor is large (hits the 1.10 clip) and hurts, showing that in-sample retransformation calibration does not transfer across periods. Any of these is informative; (b)/(c) would be recorded negative results. Chronological block diagnostics are computed and reported but explicitly NOT used to select, so the selected branch is fixed and re-fitting on train+development cannot silently switch it.

proposals.hypothesis: Question: is the 2011->2012 growth in hourly rentals representable as an approximately multiplicative (additive-in-log) level shift that a boosted tree cannot extrapolate, and does making that trend explicit transfer better into a later period than letting the tree split on elapsed_day/yr? Prior evidence that changed my view: the raw-target reference HGB scored development RMSE 59.99 (idea-baseline-2) / 59.98 (idea-7637c7) while the identical settings on log1p(cnt) scored 51.88 (idea-7da84f), i.e. the multiplicative/variance-stabilising assumption gave the single largest measured gain so far, and that program's own findings report 100% of development rows lie beyond the training elapsed_day range with a fitted retransformation factor of only 1.026 and a chronological block where predicted mean (270.7) exceeded actual (242.2). Trees are piecewise constant in elapsed_day, so beyond the training span they must reuse the last learned level; if growth is genuinely separable in log space, an explicit clipped linear log-trend fitted to out-of-fold daily residuals of a model that never sees elapsed_day/yr should recover the missing level and reduce row RMSE. Contrasting expected outcomes stated before execution: (a) if growth is separable and under-extrapolated, branch B alone beats branch A on development and the fixed 0.5/0.5 blend lands below 51.88; (b) if the tree already absorbs the year effect through yr/mnth/season splits, the extrapolated trend overshoots the observed level and the blend sits between ~52 and ~56, which would be an informative negative result against the separable-growth representation; (c) if development level noise dominates, the blend differs from 51.88 by less than ~1 RMSE and the seed averaging (3 seeds, log space) is the only remaining effect. This is an exploratory joint change (seed averaging + detrended branch + trend extrapolation + fixed 0.5 weight), so it does not support single-factor attribution; the program therefore reports branch-A, branch-B and blend errors separately on an interpolation fold set and on a chronological last-40-date block, both labelled diagnostic-only, with the branch fixed a priori because the parent's findings state that this spring block previously mis-ranked candidates relative to actual train->development transfer. Slope is clipped to [0, 0.0012] per day and the extrapolated log increment beyond the last training date to 0.15, bounding the damage if hypothesis (b) holds, including after the final refit on train+development where confirmation days extend much further.

scientific_limits: Returns to a separable growth question despite direct frozen-trend failure; differs in log residual estimator, clipping, seed averaging and blend, so it is a new joint method, not a replicated single-factor test.

proposals.hypothesis: Question: on the May-June 2012 development period, does modelling log1p(cnt) with explicit hour-cycle and hour-by-workingday interaction features transfer better than the recorded plain-count HistGradientBoosting reference (action d81da712..., dev row RMSE 59.99, equal-date MAE 40.95)? Prior evidence changed my view about the size of the gap to close: the recorded median-like and Ridge-like references (268.48 and 182.95) show that hourly rentals are dominated by a strongly non-additive hour x workingday pattern, and the tree reference already captures most of it, so a feature-only tweak is unlikely to be decisive by itself. Contrasting expected outcomes stated before execution: (a) log1p training reduces relative error at night/low-count hours but systematically shrinks peak-hour predictions and therefore WORSENS squared-error RMSE relative to the raw-count reference, in which case the program should select a raw-count branch and I will report this as an informative negative result about the loss/target mismatch; (b) log1p with a Duan smearing back-transform recovers the peak level and beats the raw reference on RMSE; (c) neither target matters much and the engineered cycle/interaction columns alone give a small gain; (d) dropping elapsed_day helps because trees cannot extrapolate a calendar index past the training range (train ends 2012-04-30), or hurts because elapsed_day carries the 2011->2012 growth level. Selection is made by the program itself using two purely forward-in-time date-blocked holdouts carved from the training dates (last 61 dates, and the preceding 61 dates), so the internal comparison measures future-period transfer rather than interpolation; the refit on train(+development for the final fixed source) may change the selected branch, and the findings report exactly which branch, smearing factor and any fallback were used. Unverified/exploratory: the smearing factor is estimated from in-sample residuals and is expected to be optimistic.

proposals.hypothesis: Question: does the level/growth information carried by elapsed_day transfer into a later period better when represented as an explicit additive log-scale trend that can extrapolate, rather than as a raw tree split feature that saturates at the last training bin? Evidence that shaped this: in the recorded development leader (action 617ee9b8..., idea-aa2bb2, dev RMSE 55.97, group MAE 36.49) the internal time-blocked comparison showed that deleting the elapsed_day column while keeping day-of-year harmonics cost a lot (log_eng_noed mean fold RMSE 114.05 vs log_eng 91.17 with the column, log_eng_smear 89.17), so season+yr+doy alone do not supply the level; yet an HGB split on elapsed_day cannot extend a trend past the training range, and the selection margin between the two best branches there was tiny (89.17 vs 90.16 over only two folds), so the internal ranking is weakly resolved. That leader also showed internal fold RMSE (~89) far above the actual development RMSE (56), i.e. fold difficulty is not directly comparable to the dev period, so only relative branch ordering is used here. Contrasting expected outcomes stated before execution: (a) if tree saturation plus the yr indicator already absorbs the 2012 level, direct_ed wins on all folds and especially on the added long-horizon fold, and the explicit-trend branches are equal or worse - an informative negative result against trend extrapolation; (b) if within-2012 growth continues roughly linearly, trend_damp/trend_full beat direct_ed mainly on the long-horizon fold (61-122 day ahead), which is the regime closest to the July-December confirmation period after refitting on train+development; (c) if the fitted residual slope is near zero, trend_freeze (level frozen at the last training day) matches direct_ed and no_trend stays clearly worse, confirming that a level term is needed but not a slope. Joint change is declared: the trend branches both drop the raw elapsed_day column and add the residual trend, so a win cannot be attributed to a single factor; trend_freeze vs trend_full isolates the extrapolation slope with everything else fixed (same HGB hyperparameters, same engineered features, same log1p target and smearing as the parent's selected branch). Program-reported findings and the selected branch may still be wrong; the fitted intercept/slope, per-fold RMSE/MAE of every branch and any fallback use are reported so the next decision can distinguish interpolation from future-period transfer.

proposals.hypothesis: Question: does the residual structure that transfers into a later period depend on the training objective (log1p-Gaussian with smearing vs native Poisson deviance on counts) and on how much weight recent dates get, or is the parent's log+smearing branch already the transferring representation? Prior evidence: idea-aa2bb2 and idea-c96575 produce byte-identical development results (loss 55.967, group MAE 36.49) because both internally selected the same log1p+engineered-features+smearing HGB with elapsed_day retained; c96575's added trend-extrapolation branches were effectively no-ops (fitted slopes ~1e-5 per day) and the no-elapsed_day branch was clearly worse (internal mean RMSE 114 vs 89), so tree-flat extrapolation of elapsed_day (freezing the 2012 level) currently carries the level shift. That evidence changed my view: explicit linear trend extrapolation is not the lever, so this round tests the error model and sample weighting instead. Contrasting expected outcomes: (a) Poisson loss beats log+smearing because hourly counts are heteroscedastic and the smearing factor (1.019) is a crude global correction, giving lower development RMSE; (b) log+smearing remains best and Poisson is worse at peak hours, i.e. an informative negative result about the error model; (c) recency weighting (180-day half-life) helps most because the later period's level and commuting profile resemble 2012 more than 2011, or it hurts by discarding the 2011 same-season signal needed for May-June. Seed averaging over 3 seeds is included for all multi-seed branches to reduce fit noise; the single-seed log branch is kept as an explicit replicate of the parent's selected configuration so the seed-averaging effect is visible, not confounded. Validation is changed to only 61-day-horizon blocked folds (the deployment horizon) with a 0.65/0.35 recency weight, because the parent's 122-day fold (h2_long61, internal RMSE ~124-155) dominated its averaged criterion while actual development RMSE was 56, indicating the long-horizon fold is not representative of the scored protocol. This is exploratory and jointly varies objective, weights and seed averaging across branches; the findings report per-branch, per-fold RMSE/MAE so branch-level attribution is possible, and the selected branch plus any fallback are reported explicitly.

scientific_limits: Complete training-only objective/recency/seed factorial comparisons; direct log one-seed branch replicates prior selected configuration for this seed.

Calls 61-day development horizon the deployment horizon and discards longer-horizon fold although final July-December spans 184 days; short development success cannot establish that long-horizon diagnostics are irrelevant.

proposals.hypothesis: Question: do within-date weather aggregates (whole-day mean/max temp, humidity, wind, worst weathersit, rainy-hour fraction), adjacent-hour weather (previous/next hour conditions), or an explicit hierarchical decomposition (predicted daily total × normalized predicted hour share) represent the rental process better than the flat hourly model that the recorded runs selected? Prior evidence that changed my view: in action 527d5223... and 617ee9b8... the horizon-matched internal folds ranked log1p-target + smearing + calendar/harmonic engineering best (weighted RMSE 93.42; per-fold 103.32 / 75.02), Poisson loss was clearly worse (111.38), recency weighting with 180-day half-life was worse (96.66), and dropping elapsed_day was much worse (mean RMSE 114.05 vs 89.17), i.e. a trend/level feature is needed. Actual development row RMSE for the selected branch was 55.97 with equal-date MAE 36.49, far below internal fold RMSE, so internal folds (March-April dates) are systematically harder than the May-June development window; internal scores are therefore usable only as a ranking signal, not as a level estimate. That gap made me stop tuning the same flat GBM hyperparameters and instead test competing representational assumptions. Contrasting expected outcomes stated before execution: (a) day-level weather context plus adjacent-hour weather improves internal weighted RMSE by >2% relative to the flat replicate, which would mean people's hourly decisions respond to the day's overall and recent weather rather than only the concurrent hour; (b) no improvement or a regression, which would be an informative negative result that the supplied concurrent-hour normalized weather already carries the transferable weather signal; (c) the hierarchical day-total × hour-share model beats both flats, supporting level/shape separation as the transferable structure, or (more likely in my current view) it loses because share normalization forces each date's total onto a single day-level prediction and propagates day-level error to every hour. A 2-of-3-component average is also scored so that an ensemble option can win only if it actually improves the same horizon-matched internal criterion. Transductive use is explicit: day aggregates, neighbour-hour lookups and hour-share normalization use unlabeled evaluation covariates grouped by date; no evaluation labels are used anywhere. The program reports the branch it actually selects, its internal score, the flat replicate score and any fallback use, so a valid vector cannot silently impersonate the intended component.

scientific_limits: Distinct representation research: daily-context features, adjacent weather and hierarchical daily-total times normalized hourly share; flat parent is an actual comparable branch.
A gain from aggregate weather cannot establish that people respond causally to daily/recent weather; correlated covariates and missing-hour structure remain.
Uses whole evaluation-day weather including later hours and observed-hour count; valid conditional batch prediction, not operational real-time forecasting.
Hierarchy changes model structure and hyperparameters jointly, while flat_rep vs flat_day is more controlled. Retains short-horizon criterion and unreported zero substitution.
source_review.scope: Entire expanded source read; training-only labels for daily totals and hour-share models; explicit unlabeled evaluation date grouping/weather use; no I/O.

proposals.hypothesis: Question: the round-4 leader (action 87311d22..., task idea-e8e22d) selected the flat_day_neigh representation because its internal horizon-matched weighted fold RMSE (85.2) beat flat_rep (93.4), flat_day (88.0), hier_day_share (103.8) and all blends (90.3-93.0); yet its actual development row RMSE was 47.75, roughly half the fold estimate. That large level mismatch means the internal folds (validation on Jan-Apr 2012 dates) are a much harder/higher-variance regime than May-June 2012, so I no longer trust that the fold ranking direction transfers - previously I assumed it did, which is exactly what the selection rule inside the program depends on. This analysis uses the analyze channel, which legitimately receives train AND development X/y/groups, to measure directly (a) train-only-fit development RMSE / MAE / equal-date MAE for flat_rep, flat_day, flat_day_neigh and three new variants (exponential recency weighting with 120-day and 60-day half-life, and a raw-count instead of log1p+smearing target), (b) the same candidates' internal fold scores so fold-vs-development rank agreement can be checked, and (c) residual diagnostics: signed bias overall, by hour bucket, over the two development months, daily-total prediction/actual ratio, and the effect of a multiplicative level factor estimated only from the last 28 train dates (held out from its own fit). Contrasting expected outcomes stated before execution: (1) agreement outcome - development ranking reproduces the fold ranking with flat_day_neigh best, near-zero daily-total bias, and recency weighting / level calibration changing development RMSE by <3%; then the fold rule is validated and round 6 should simply select the recorded leader. (2) disagreement outcome - flat_day or a blend beats flat_day_neigh on development, and/or the model shows systematic under-prediction of daily totals in the later period (growth/level drift that tree splits on elapsed_day cannot extrapolate), with recency weighting or a level factor cutting development RMSE by >=3%; then round 6 should submit a revised method embedding the winning adjustment. Either result is informative: outcome (1) is a negative result that still de-risks the final fixed source. Validity limits acknowledged up front: any development-measured gain is in-sample with respect to the mechanical selection metric, only one city/one 61-day window is involved, the final source is refitted on train+development so an internally selected branch may change, day-aggregate and neighbour-hour features are transductive over unlabeled covariates of the scored period, and nothing here tests July-December confirmation transfer.

scientific_limits: Diagnostic directly compares development ranking with training fold ranking and admits final transfer remains untested; analysis has legitimate development-label access.

proposals.hypothesis: Question: is the residual error of the current development leader (idea-e8e22d, flat_day_neigh, dev row RMSE 47.75, equal-date MAE 32.71) dominated by an inability of trees to extrapolate calendar level beyond the training range, and can an explicit 2011 seasonal profile plus a year-over-year growth term repair it? Prior evidence changed my view twice. (a) The recorded analysis 1d0f99d8 showed horizon-matched folds have huge negative bias (h1_last61 bias -53.4, h1_prev61 -50.3, weighted RMSE 85.2) while the actual development window had only bias -10.1 and RMSE 47.75, and development underprediction grew with date (first-half bias -3.69 vs second-half -16.37, daily pred/actual median 0.945). So the deficit is not random noise, it is a level/season extrapolation deficit whose size depends on how far the target period sits past the last trained calendar position. (b) The same analysis showed a constant level factor estimated from a 28-day internal tail was 0.9920 and made development RMSE 1.09% WORSE, so a scalar recency calibration is refuted as the fix. This proposal therefore tests a structured correction instead: a smoothed 2011 daily log-level profile S(doy) (+-10 day window) plus a robust median year-over-year offset g estimated from the 2012 training dates, applied either as a log-space offset on the target (genuine extrapolation) or as an extra feature (tree-mediated, expected to inherit the same extrapolation ceiling), with recent-90-day and all-2012 variants of g, plus base/anchor blends. Contrasting expected outcomes stated before execution: (i) anchor-offset branches win the horizon-matched internal folds by a large margin (fold bias moving from about -50 toward 0) AND transfer, giving development RMSE below 47.75; (ii) anchor wins the folds but overcorrects the milder May-June gap and development RMSE rises above 47.75 - this would be an informative negative result showing horizon-matched fold ranking does not transfer for level corrections, matching the failed 0.992 calibration, and the previously measured method would remain the best development reference; (iii) anchor loses on the folds and the program selects base_dayneigh, which should closely replicate 47.75 and act as a self-consistency check of the selection machinery. The anchor uses only training labels and the supplied evaluation calendar; day-aggregate and neighbour-hour features remain transductive over unlabeled evaluation covariates grouped by date, and this is reported in findings. Unverified until executed: all expected magnitudes above are authored expectations, not measurements.

scientific_limits: Explores seasonal anchor as feature versus target offset and recent/all growth estimates, with matched base prediction rule.
Two development-half bias values do not prove the deficit is non-random calendar extrapolation; no uncertainty or alternative-cause test identifies that mechanism.
A0.992 calibration failure rejects that fitted rule, not scalar calibration generally.
Smoothed target-derived anchor includes own training labels and influences internal random early-stop targets; outer chronological holdouts remain unseen.
Late-2012 day-of-year mapping assumes a fixed365day offset, so leap-year end maps beyond prior-year support and np.interp uses boundary value.
source_review.scope: Full expanded source read; historical seasonal daily log anchor fitted only from training labels; transductive weather context declared; no I/O or evaluation labels.

proposals.hypothesis: Question: does the strong development result of the raw-target HistGradientBoosting reference (idea-baseline-2, action d81da712..., dev RMSE 59.99 vs Ridge 182.95 vs median 268.48) rest on relationships that transfer to a later period, or partly on a non-extrapolable level feature? Trees cannot extrapolate elapsed_day beyond the training range, and the raw-count target forces the model to learn hour-by-level interactions additively even though rental growth from 2011 to 2012 is plausibly multiplicative (hourly pattern scaled by a rising volume). Contrasting expected outcomes: (A) log1p target and/or dropping elapsed_day transfer better on a chronological internal holdout (last 61 training dates, future-period transfer rather than interpolation) and reduce negative bias on high-volume 2012 hours; (B) raw target wins because RMSE is dominated by peak hours and log fitting under-weights them, and elapsed_day helps by pinning the latest level via its last leaf. The program runs all 6 combinations, selects by internal holdout RMSE, refits on the full train set, and reports internal RMSE/MAE/bias, the selected branch, a 2012/2011 same-month level-ratio diagnostic, and any fallback use. Prior evidence changed my view only in that the Ridge->HGB gap shows nonlinear hour/weather structure is essential, so I keep the HGB core and vary only target scale and the trend feature. Note: early_stopping is set to False explicitly (the reference used sklearn's auto early stopping since train exceeds 10000 rows), so this is a joint change, not a one-factor attribution to the transform alone. Exploratory and unverified until executed.

source_review.scientific_limits: Explicitly acknowledges early-stopping change versus measured reference. Six internal comparisons share model settings but only one seasonal holdout; log inverse is not conditional-mean correction. Same-month year means mix observed weather/calendar/composition effects and do not identify growth causally.
source_review.scope: Full source reviewed: six raw/log/sqrt by date-feature HGB variants, forward last61day validation, no early stopping, exact selected transform/feature findings and explicit nonfinite replacement; no I/O.

proposals.hypothesis: Question: does the 2011->2012 level shift transfer as a continuing multiplicative growth trend, a plateau, or is it already absorbed by the baseline HGB via the yr feature? Evidence: idea-59da36 (action 2d119fec...) measured internal pseudo-future holdout (cut elapsed_day 425, 61 days) with systematic negative bias for every variant (-54 to -97 rides/hour) and year_level_by_month ratios of 1.84-2.53x, i.e. trees trained mostly on 2011 underpredict later periods and elapsed_day makes it worse (raw|all rmse 115.5 vs raw|no_elapsed_day 95.2). Yet its internally selected sqrt|no_elapsed_day scored dev RMSE 63.04, worse than the plain baseline HGB with all features (idea-baseline-2, 59.99), so a single far-extrapolative holdout misranked candidates; this changed my view: level must be modeled explicitly, and internal selection should use two forward-chained 30-day folds closer to the real train/dev gap and must include the baseline itself as a candidate. Method: HGB on log1p(cnt) using shape features (all except elapsed_day and yr) plus an additive daily log-level offset estimated from cross-fitted (5 contiguous date blocks) out-of-block daily mean residuals; offset for future days is 'none', 'const60' (mean of last 60 training days), 'trend_all' (linear in elapsed_day over all training days) or 'trend180' (linear over last 180 days). Contrasting expected outcomes: (A) trend variants win internally and reduce dev RMSE below 59.99 with pred_mean well above train_mean -> growth continues and is transferable; (B) const60 wins -> level shift transfers as a plateau, trend extrapolation overshoots (positive bias); (C) baseline_all_raw wins or level variants show larger dev RMSE -> the yr indicator already captures the transferable level and residual-level modeling adds noise. Findings report all fold metrics, fitted slopes/constants, the actually selected branch after refitting and any fallback. Unverified exploratory reasoning; a joint change (log target + feature drop + offset), so one-factor attribution is not claimed.

scientific_limits: Fits log residual level using blocked cross-fitting within training; outer chronological holds remain unseen. Inner blocks use later training dates, so residuals are not prospective forecast errors.
baseline_all_raw disables early stopping, unlike the measured reference; claimed baseline candidate is not an exact control.
Joint log-target, feature-removal and residual-trend change acknowledged; two 30-day folds do not match 184-day final horizon.

findings.design: fixed submission; internal chronological folds are diagnostics only, not used for selection

proposals.hypothesis: Question: recorded rentals grew strongly from 2011 to early 2012 (train mean 154 vs last-60-day mean 232 in idea-f87923 findings). Which representation of that level shift transfers into May-June 2012? Prior evidence: idea-baseline-2 (squared-error HGB, all features incl. elapsed_day and yr, dev RMSE 59.99, group MAE 40.95) is the best valid measurement; idea-f87923's detached additive log1p level offset (const60=+0.55, i.e. ~1.74x on a shape model trained without yr/elapsed_day) selected by a 2-fold internal comparison overshot badly on dev (pred_mean 334, RMSE 93.3), and its two internal folds disagreed on the sign of the raw baseline's bias (-45 vs +8). This changed my view: bolting a separately estimated level onto a shape model plus small-fold selection is fragile; the level should be learned jointly with the covariates, and internal folds should serve as diagnostics, not as the selector. Proposal: hold every baseline-2 hyperparameter fixed (max_iter=250, lr=0.08, max_leaf_nodes=31, l2=1, random_state=1729, default early_stopping='auto', which with >10000 rows is likely active; n_iter_ is reported) and change only loss='poisson', submitting that model with all features. Contrasting expectations: (A) if rentals scale multiplicatively (hour/weather shape x growth level), the Poisson link lets the same trees represent the yr/elapsed_day effect as a ratio and dev RMSE falls below 59.99 with reduced |bias| on the recorded holdouts; (B) if dev error is dominated by high-count hourly noise, Poisson deviance down-weights large-count errors and dev RMSE is equal or worse (an informative negative for the multiplicative-transfer view). Diagnostics only (no selection): three chronological 30-day holdouts (cuts at last-90/-60/-30 train days) comparing squared_all, poisson_all and poisson without elapsed_day, reporting RMSE/MAE/bias/pred_mean per fold, plus the Jan-Apr 2012/2011 mean ratio to expose the raw growth factor. Any fit failure falls back to squared_error and is reported in findings. One city and one 61-day period cannot establish general benefit.

scientific_limits: Fixed Poisson submission with chronological diagnostic folds; direct objective comparison retains baseline hyperparameters and original features, except zero clipping of predictions.
Correctly notes previous separately fitted offset overshot and that early stopping is automatic. Internal folds are diagnostics, not selectors.
Failure of a Poisson learner would not disprove multiplicative structure generally; a link-function comparison is narrower.

proposals.hypothesis: Question: the development leader idea-a0bc19 (Poisson HGB, all features, loss 54.01, group MAE 35.89) recorded jan_apr_level_ratio_2012_over_2011 = 2.10 and a fold at cut_426 with bias -49 (holdout mean 222 vs pred mean 173), while trees cannot extrapolate elapsed_day beyond day 485 (eval range 486-546). Does an explicit multiplicative growth offset L(day)=exp(b*(day-last_train_day)), with b estimated only from year-over-year matched daily mean-hourly ratios in the fitting window, transfer into the later period? Contrasting expected outcomes: (A) growth continues -> full offset (damp 1.0) removes the negative bias seen at later cuts, internal 61-day-horizon folds and development RMSE fall below 54; (B) growth saturated or startup-inflated (Jan-Apr 2011 was ramp-up) -> full offset overshoots with positive bias, damp 0.5 or 0.0 wins internally and any dev gain is small or negative; (C) the internal selection is unstable across the three folds, indicating the growth signal is too noisy for a 61-day horizon. Evidence changed my view: the parent's fold bias pattern (-49 at cut_426 but +5 at cut_456) means growth is not uniform, so the program selects a damping factor in {0, 0.5, 1} by mean RMSE over three chronological folds with a 61-day horizon matching development, and reports the selected branch, the estimated b, implied annual factor and implied factor at eval mid-point. This is a joint change (target normalization + internal selection) relative to the parent; same HGB hyperparameters and features are held fixed. Unverified exploratory rationale; a dev gain would need confirmation-period transfer.

proposals.hypothesis: Question: do older (2011 start-up regime) hourly records help or hurt transfer to a later period when the model is otherwise fixed? Evidence so far: the development leader idea-a0bc19 (plain Poisson HGB, all features, uniform weights) scored loss 54.01 / group MAE 35.89 with pred_mean 264.3 vs train_last60_mean 232.5; its child idea-2a518e imposed an explicit exponential YoY growth factor (selected damp 1.0, implied factor 1.068 at eval mid, pred_mean 296.5) and got worse (65.18 / 41.55), so explicit level extrapolation overshot even though its internal folds preferred it. Both programs' internal spring fold (cut ~425) showed about -100 bias for every variant, i.e. a level jump no candidate captured, which makes the internal fold mean a weak selector. This changed my view: instead of extrapolating a trend, test whether de-emphasizing the early-2011 regime (recency sample weights with half-life in {none,365,180,90} days, weights normalized to mean 1, identical hparams and features to idea-a0bc19) lets the tree model learn a level/profile closer to the recent regime without extrapolation. Contrasting expected outcomes: (A) if 2011 relationships transfer well, hl_none wins internally and dev loss stays ~54 -- an informative negative result that the full history is worth keeping; (B) if the ramp-up regime distorts learned levels, hl_180 or hl_90 wins internally and dev loss drops below 54 with pred_mean modestly above 264; (C) a possible regression: weighting shrinks effective sample size (reported per fold) and could raise variance, giving worse dev RMSE even if internal folds favor it, as happened with idea-2a518e. Selection is by mean RMSE over 3 chronological 61-day-horizon folds with ties resolved toward uniform weights; the program reports the selected half-life, per-fold results, effective sample sizes and any fallback. Single-factor design: only sample weights vary.

Recorded evidence: a0bc19 internal folds gave poisson_all 60.80 vs squared_all 60.96 mean RMSE with opposite-signed biases in cut_396/cut_456, suggesting partially complementary errors; poisson_no_elapsed was worse (63.53), so elapsed_day is kept. idea-cf138a showed recency weighting did not help (hl_none selected in all 3 folds, identical submission to a0bc19, dev RMSE 54.009), which moved my view away from time-weighting and toward representation/ensemble questions. The cut_425 fold (train through mid-March 2012, holdout Mar-Apr 2012) had bias -104 for every candidate, indicating the spring level shift is the dominant untransferred component and is unlikely to be fixed by these variants; this test is therefore bounded. Contrasting expected outcomes: (1) avg_poisson_all_squared or avg_all_three wins internal folds by 1-3% mean RMSE and submits a slightly lower dev RMSE (<54.0); (2) poisson_no_month_season wins if month effects are mostly weather proxies whose year-interaction fails to transfer; (3) poisson_all wins all folds, in which case the program submits exactly the a0bc19 predictor (ties favor it) and the informative result is that feature-subset/loss averaging does not help, leaving a0bc19 as the fixed selection. Only sample-independent model variants of the same hyperparameters vary; the selection is by mean RMSE over 3 chronological 61-day folds as in cf138a. Fallbacks are reported explicitly. proposals.hypothesis: Question: does the 2011->2012 growth in recorded rentals transfer into May-June 2012 as a multiplicative factor on the hour/weather/calendar profile, and does an additive raw-count HGB fail to carry it? Evidence: HGB (idea-baseline-2, dev RMSE 59.99, group MAE 40.95) beats standardized Ridge (182.95) and median (268.48) by a large margin, showing nonlinear hr x workingday x weather structure dominates; but raw-count HGB fits additive leaf values and cannot exceed levels seen in training, and May-June with yr=1 is an unseen mnth x yr cell. Contrasting expected outcomes: (A) if growth is a roughly stable multiplicative factor, HGB on log1p(cnt) (branch 'log') or log-detrended HGB with linear log-trend extrapolation ('log_trend', elapsed_day and yr dropped from the trees) wins the internal forward folds (last two 61-day blocks of train, fit on strictly earlier dates) and lowers dev RMSE below 59.99 without worsening equal-date MAE; (B) if growth is not stable or trend extrapolation overshoots summer 2012, 'raw' wins or log_trend regresses, which would be an informative negative about trend transfer; (C) a mismatch between the internally selected branch and the dev outcome would indicate that forward validation on Jan-Apr 2012 does not proxy the May-June transfer. The program reports the selected branch, fold RMSEs, fitted annual growth factor, any exception-based fallback to 'raw', and nonfinite replacements, so the selection can be audited. Joint change (target transform + selection) is exploratory; single-factor attribution is available only via the reported per-branch fold scores. Unverified until executed.

source_review.scientific_limits: Joint target/trend/selection change. Log trend estimated with observational calendar/weather controls is not causal growth. A boosted ensemble does not generally have predictions bounded by the training target range, although tree date effects cannot extrapolate outside their split range. Auto early stopping can differ between smaller internal fits and full refit. Infinite failure scores would violate finite findings if a branch fails.
source_review.scope: Full source reviewed: raw/log HGB and log-linear detrending, two forward date folds, selected branch and explicit exception/nonfinite reporting; no I/O.

findings.note: branch selection uses only training dates (two forward 61-day holdouts); evaluation covariates used only for final prediction; baseline HGB hyperparameters fixed

proposals.hypothesis: Question: does the hourly-rental structure transfer to a later period better as an additive (squared_error) or multiplicative (Poisson log-link, or log1p target) relationship within the same HistGradientBoosting learner? Prior evidence: idea-baseline-2 (HGB, all features, squared error) reached development RMSE 59.99 / equal-date MAE 40.95, while idea-ea0e19 dropped elapsed_day/yr and imposed a parametric log-trend, ending at 122.13 — its own forward folds showed the plain log branch was worst in the most recent fold (140.6 vs 116.6 raw), which revised my view: removing the tree's direct access to yr/elapsed_day level information hurt, and a pure log target may shrink peak-hour predictions that dominate RMSE. Contrasting expected outcomes: (A) Poisson loss keeps the multiplicative hour x working-day x weather scaling and matches or beats squared error on forward RMSE (<= ~58 on development) and improves equal-date MAE; (B) squared error remains best on RMSE because RMSE is dominated by peak counts and Poisson under-weights large residuals; (C) log1p target wins on equal-date MAE but loses on RMSE, replicating the ea0e19 pattern. The program selects the branch by mean RMSE over two forward 61-day holdouts using only training dates, reports per-branch fold RMSE and per-date MAE, refits the selected branch on all training rows, and reports any fallback. Only baseline HGB hyperparameters are held fixed, so a single factor (objective/target transform) is varied. Unverified exploratory expectation; one city/two years cannot establish general benefit.

scientific_limits: Three objectives use otherwise matching HGB hyperparameters and original features; all fit and select only on training labels.
Prior error cannot establish that removing date/year caused degradation because detrending and target also changed.
Internal nonfinite replacement is not counted and failed-fold infinity would invalidate strict findings JSON; inspect actual execution.
source_review.scope: Complete expanded source read by operator; numerical sklearn/numpy only; training-label-only fit/selection, no I/O, bounded CPU action.

findings.note: growth rate b fitted on log daily totals of training dates only (trend + 2 harmonics); target deflated by exp(b*(day-last_train_day)) and predictions re-inflated; branch selection by mean RMSE over two forward 61-day training holdouts; HGB hyperparameters fixed at baseline; evaluation covariates used only for final prediction

proposals.hypothesis: Question: the parent (idea-ae78bf, action 8305d9ba...) kept the baseline HGB (squared branch selected; dev RMSE 59.976 vs baseline 59.993, effectively unchanged) and showed forward-holdout RMSE far worse than development (fold1 days 424-485: 116.6; fold2: 74.9). Tree models predict a flat level beyond the training day range, so a continuing 2011->2012 growth trend cannot be extrapolated by elapsed_day/yr splits; the log1p and poisson branches, which encode multiplicative structure, were nevertheless worse on those forward folds, so a pure loss change is not the fix. This program tests a separable trend: fit log daily totals on training dates only as a + b*day + two day-of-year harmonics, deflate the target by exp(b*(day-last_train_day)), fit the same fixed-hyperparameter squared-error HGB on the deflated target, and re-inflate predictions with the extrapolated factor. Two deflated variants (drop yr/elapsed_day so the trend must live in the deflator; keep all features) are compared with the unchanged squared branch using the parent's two forward 61-day holdouts, with b re-estimated inside each fold. Contrasting expected outcomes: (A) if the level shift is a persistent exponential trend, deflated branches cut forward-fold RMSE materially (fold1 well below 116) and the program selects a deflated branch, giving dev RMSE below 59.98; (B) if growth has saturated or is seasonal confounding, the deflator over-predicts, deflated branches lose on forward folds, the program keeps 'squared' and the dev result matches the parent, an informative negative result about trend transfer. Findings expose the estimated daily growth rate and implied annual factor per fold and for the final refit, so the selected branch and its trend assumption are visible. Note the branch selection is by forward-holdout RMSE only; a 5% dev gain from this single 61-day period would still not establish transfer to July-December. Unverified until executed.

scientific_limits: Returns to growth after failed round1 log trend; modified daily-total growth and raw ratio loss are distinct but original counterexample is not discussed.
Daily totals also reflect missing recorded hours; harmonic separation is not causal identification of growth.
Deflated target is fitted without scale-squared weights, so objective changes; feature removal is separate branch.
Original reference has unclipped predictions; this program compares against round2 clipped reference. Failed-fold infinities can invalidate findings; inspect execution.
source_review.scope: Full expanded source read; numerical training-only daily-total trend, ratio regression and chronological comparisons; no I/O.

findings.note: lag features are training-label counts at elapsed_day-364 same hr (point) or mean of lag 357/364/371 same hr plus mean daily total over lag week (smooth); NaN when unavailable; tables built only from the fold/final training labels; branch selection by mean RMSE over two forward 61-day training holdouts; fold 2 training rows have no lag so its lag branches cannot learn lag relations; HGB hyperparameters fixed at baseline; evaluation covariates used only for final prediction

proposals.hypothesis: Question: does the level relationship between a 2012 hour and the same hour one year (52 weeks, weekday-aligned) earlier transfer into the later period better than (a) letting trees infer level from yr/elapsed_day alone or (b) a global exponential trend? Prior evidence changed my view: idea-816bb1 fitted a global log-linear trend (annual factor 2.16 on train-only daily totals) and deflated/re-inflated targets; it degraded development RMSE to 81.03 vs 59.98 for the fixed-HGB leader idea-ae78bf (which itself matched baseline-2 at 59.99, so target-transform branches added nothing). This suggests a global multiplicative growth extrapolation overshoots, while trees using yr already carry most of the transferable level. Instead of extrapolating a trend, this program supplies a local anchor: for each row, the training-label rental count at elapsed_day-364 with the same hr ('lag_point'), and a smoothed version averaging the same hour at lag 357/364/371 plus the mean daily total over the week around lag 364 ('lag_smooth'), both alongside the original covariates; missing values (all 2011 rows) are left NaN for HGB. Branches base/lag_point/lag_smooth use identical fixed baseline HGB hyperparameters and are selected by mean RMSE over two forward 61-day training holdouts exactly as in idea-ae78bf, so the only changed factor per branch is the feature set. Contrasting expectations: if the previous-year hourly relationship transfers, lag_smooth should beat base in fold 1 (holdout Mar-Apr 2012, the only fold where training rows carry lags) and development RMSE should fall below ~57 (>=5% relative gain) without equal-date MAE worsening; if the lag columns act mainly as a yr proxy confounded with missingness, or previous-year weather noise dominates, the gain will be nil (~60) or negative, which would be an informative negative about year-over-year hourly transfer. Fold 2 (holdout Jan-Feb 2012) cannot learn lag relationships because all its training rows are 2011; this is reported rather than hidden. The program also reports train-only year-over-year monthly daily-total ratios for Jan-Apr 2012 vs 2011 to check the 2.16 annual factor assumed by idea-816bb1. Program-authored findings are diagnostics on training data only, not evaluation-label metrics.

scientific_limits: Introduces year-ago local anchors after global trend failure; a distinct representation, not evidence of literature novelty.
Lag branches change two features together; missingness and year coverage may drive differences.
Claim of no lag features in the older training fold is exact for point lag but smoothed daily feature may be available near year end; reported fractions govern actual coverage.
Two61day folds are short relative to184day final; failed-fold infinity behavior retained.
source_review.scope: Complete source read; annual lag tables use only passed training labels, every lookup is at least357days before target, no unseen evaluation targets or I/O.

findings.note: yoy_scaled: HGB (baseline hyperparameters, squared error) fit on cnt divided by a +/-14-day smoothed mean hourly count per training date; evaluation-date level = smoothed level at elapsed_day-364 times geometric-mean YoY ratio over trailing 56 training days (clipped to [0.5,4]); persistence of last training level when no analog; blend = 0.5*(base+yoy_scaled); selection by mean forward RMSE over training folds with analog coverage >= 50 percent (all folds if none); only evaluation elapsed_day is used for analog lookup; no evaluation labels anywhere

proposals.hypothesis: Question: is the forward-transfer error of the HGB reference dominated by the aggregate rental LEVEL (growth between periods) rather than by the within-day/weather shape? Evidence that changed my view: idea-325a52 (valid, dev loss 59.976, base branch selected) reported forward fold 1 RMSE 116.6 for base HGB (train through day 424, holdout Mar-Apr 2012) versus 59.98 on development, and a 2012-vs-2011 daily-total ratio of 2.14 overall (Jan 2.51, Feb 2.03, Mar 2.55, Apr 1.78). Lag COUNTS as extra covariates (lag_point/lag_smooth) did not help because a tree cannot learn a lag relation for rows lacking lag support and cannot extrapolate level beyond seen yr/elapsed_day values. idea-ae78bf showed log1p/poisson losses did not beat squared error, so this program keeps squared-error HGB with baseline hyperparameters and instead changes the REPRESENTATION: target z = cnt / S(date), where S is a centered +/-14-day smoothed mean hourly count from training labels only; HGB fits z on features without yr/elapsed_day; the evaluation-date level is extrapolated as S(date-364)*r with r the geometric-mean YoY ratio of smoothed levels over the trailing 56 training days (clipped to [0.5,4] and reported), falling back to the last training level (persistence) when no analog exists, with the persistence fraction reported. Branches: base (reference HGB), yoy_scaled, blend (0.5/0.5). Contrasting expected outcomes: (A) if level shift is the main transferable error, yoy_scaled beats base clearly on fold 1 (where base was 116.6) and on development, and blend or yoy_scaled is selected with dev RMSE below 59.98; (B) if 2012 growth decelerates (April ratio 1.78 vs ~2.1 earlier) the trailing ratio over-scales, yoy_scaled is worse than base and base is re-selected, giving an informative negative result (dev loss expected to reproduce ~59.98). Pre-stated selection rule: branch with lowest mean forward RMSE over the training folds where the analog level had >=50% coverage (fold 2 has no 364-day analog in training, as 325a52 noted, so it is excluded from selection when unsupported); selection over all folds is also reported. Confirmation caveat: after refit on train+dev the level for Jul-Dec 2012 will be Jul-Dec 2011 levels times a May-Jun 2012 ratio, so any further deceleration of growth would hurt; equal-date MAE of the selected branch is reported per fold to watch the milestone constraint. Transductive use of evaluation covariates: only elapsed_day of evaluation rows is used to look up analog training levels; no evaluation labels exist in any lookup.

scientific_limits: Changes representation to smoothed daily level times normalized shape and seasonal analog; training-derived level contains own target but outer held-out labels are excluded.
Own-label smoothing enters random early-stop training/validation targets, so that internal stopping signal is not independent of level estimation; outer chronological folds remain valid.
Older fold has no fitted YoY ratio, not no year-ago development analog. Availability claim conflates training support and prediction lookup.
Selects only supported fold(s), potentially one; log/Poisson failure was an internal ranking result, not a direct development measurement of those branches.

Operator correction for prior round4: smoothing thresholds require at least4days/2hours; through day363 there are at most3days/1hour available, so no earlier-fold lag feature. Prior review suspicion was overly broad.
source_review.scope: Complete expanded source read; numerical-only operations on allowed train/development data; no I/O or final labels.

findings.note: same two forward 61-day training holdouts as idea-ae78bf; candidates: baseline HGB, slower/more regularized HGB, and date-bootstrap bags (6 bags, whole-date resampling via sample_weight multiplicity) of each; squared error throughout; selection by mean forward RMSE, ties by branch order; evaluation covariates used only for final prediction; no evaluation labels

proposals.hypothesis: Question: is the remaining development error of the HGB leader dominated by estimator variance/capacity (fixable by bagging or a slower, more regularized boosting schedule) or by period-level shift (not fixable without level extrapolation)? Contrasting expectations: (A) variance/capacity dominates -> a date-bootstrap bag of 6 HGBs or a 600-iteration lr=0.04 min_samples_leaf=40 HGB lowers development RMSE by roughly 1-4% versus 59.98; (B) transfer/level shift dominates -> all branches stay within about 1% of the leader and forward-fold RMSE remains far above development RMSE, confirming that interpolation-style variance reduction does not address the transfer gap. How prior evidence changed my view: idea-ae78bf showed loss/target transforms are not the lever (59.976 vs baseline HGB 59.993, essentially identical), and idea-fa3d93 showed that aggressive YoY level scaling selected by forward folds (yoy_ratio 2.09, blend chosen, forward fold RMSE 71 vs base 117) badly hurt development RMSE (99.8 vs 60), so within-training forward folds overstate the level gap that the final model (which sees Jan-Apr 2012) actually faces. I therefore stop pursuing level extrapolation and run the conservative check; bootstrap by whole dates respects within-date dependence. Selection uses the same two 61-day forward holdouts as idea-ae78bf so the selection protocol is held fixed; only the candidate set changes. Unverified exploratory rationale; if worse than the leader the default lowest-development-RMSE selection still applies.

scientific_limits: Whole-date bootstrap addresses within-date dependence; no evaluation labels. Final branch selection remains training-only.

Bootstrap represents multiplicities by sample weights and drops zero-weight rows, changing unique sample size and auto-early-stopping behavior; benefit cannot be attributed solely to variance reduction.
Slow branch jointly changes iteration count, rate and minimum leaf size. Claims no benefit from objectives based on previously unselected branches remain too broad.

Fits all four final branches even though only one vector is submitted; final_rmse_vs_base measures prediction difference, not label error. Initial nonfinite replacements occur before reported final count.
source_review.scope: Complete source read; numerical training-only prediction process and diagnostics, no I/O, no final or development labels passed to fit_predict.

scope: Unblinded operator assessment written after all model decisions and before final data capture or scoring. Source reviews and program findings are retained separately; provenance does not certify interpretation.
